tips.title: Four papers, a quarter each
tips.body: Speaking, Listening, Reading and Writing are **25% each** and **50 marks each** — 200 marks in all. No paper counts for more than another, so the one you like least is worth exactly as much as the one you like best.

tips.title: Answer in English where the question is in English
tips.body: In **Listening Section A** and the whole **Reading** paper the questions are set in English and answered in English. The specification says students produce all responses in English there, so a French answer does not do the job. Check the language of the question before you write a word.

tips.title: Translation into English needs every word
tips.body: In Reading you translate a French passage into English. **Every word and every tense has to be accounted for** — a phrase left out loses its mark even if the rest is perfect. Translate it all, then read your English back to check it sounds natural.

tips.title: The dictation is heard three times
tips.body: Listening Section B plays the dictation **3 times**, with pauses between sentences: use the first to hear the whole sentence, the second to fill the gaps, the third to check spelling, accents and silent endings. Knowing the pattern in advance is half the technique.

tips.title: Fifteen minutes to prepare the speaking
tips.body: Speaking gives you **15 minutes** of preparation — 14 in the invigilation room and **1 in the exam room to say the read aloud out loud**. That last minute is the only chance to hear the hard words before they count, so use it.

why.matters: Four papers, 50 marks each, a quarter of the grade apiece: the shape of the exam is worth a topic because most lost marks are lost to the shape, not the French. Answering in French where the specification asks for English responses throws away what you understood. Missing the prompt that says *ask a question* loses a mark before you open your mouth. Not knowing that the dictation is heard three times wastes the first hearing. This topic exists to make the four papers familiar before Year 11 practises them in earnest, so that the only thing left to do on the day is the French.

examples.title: Twelve marks for reading aloud
examples.body: At both tiers the read aloud is 12 of the speaking paper's 50 marks, leaving 38 for the role play and the picture task together. It is the most predictable task in the whole exam: a short text, fifteen minutes to prepare, the last of them in the exam room to practise out loud. Pronunciation earns 8 of the 12 marks, and silent endings, liaisons and nasal vowels are what it rewards; the other 4 come from answering two unprepared questions about the text, so rehearse short opinions as well as sounds.

props.caption: The speaking paper's 50 marks, at both tiers

visual.alt: Two bars to scale: twelve marks for the read aloud against thirty-eight for the role play and picture task, out of fifty for the speaking paper

examples.title: English question, English answer
examples.body: The listening and reading papers set their questions in English and want the answers in English, and the writing paper gives its instructions in English and wants the answers in French. It sounds too obvious to lose marks on, and it is the single biggest avoidable loss in the exam: a candidate who has just heard a French recording writes the French words down. Check the language of the question before you write, every time. The translation into English is the same rule with a whole passage.

examples.title: Heard three times
examples.body: The dictation is played three times, with pauses between sentences, and the three hearings have three jobs. The first is for the whole sentence, roughly written. The second fills the gaps. The third is for checking the things the ear cannot settle: accents, the silent *-ent* on a plural verb, an agreement on an adjective. Treating the first hearing as the only one is how a candidate runs out of time; treating the third as a check is how the grammar goes in.

steps.title: Les quatre épreuves
steps.body:
GCSE French is **four papers**, each worth **50 marks** and **25%** of the grade — 200 marks in all. You sit every paper at the same tier, Foundation or Higher.

**Paper 1 — Speaking** (Higher 10 to 12 minutes, Foundation 7 to 9, after 15 minutes' preparation). Three tasks in a fixed order: a **read aloud** with a short interaction after it (**12 marks**: 8 for reading aloud, 4 for answering two questions), a **role play** (**10**), and a **picture task** (**28**).

**Paper 2 — Listening** (Higher 60 minutes, Foundation 45, each including 5 minutes' reading time). **Section A** (40 marks) is comprehension: questions in English, answers in English. **Section B** (10 marks) is a **dictation**: a short French passage, played 3 times with pauses between sentences, written down in French.

**Paper 3 — Reading** (Higher 60 minutes, Foundation 45). Questions in English, answers in English, plus a **translation into English**: one passage at Higher, five sentences at Foundation.

**Paper 4 — Writing** (Higher 1 hour 20, Foundation 1 hour 15). Instructions in English, answers in French. At Higher: an informal task of **80 to 90 words**, a formal task of **130 to 150 words**, and a translation into French. At Foundation: four sentences about a photo, a formal task of **40 to 50 words**, an informal task of **80 to 90 words**, and five sentences to translate into French.

The GCSE has three **assessment objectives**, and they cut across the papers: understanding and responding to spoken French (35%), understanding and responding to written French (45%), and accurate grammar and vocabulary (20%). Each **paper** is still 25%, so there is no paper to neglect.

steps.title: Répondre en anglais
steps.body:
The commonest avoidable loss of marks in GCSE French is answering in **the wrong language**.

**Listening Section A and the whole Reading paper** set their questions **in English** and expect answers **in English**. The specification says all questions are set in English and students produce all responses in English in those sections, so write the meaning in English, however good your French is. Before you write, look at the language of the question.

**Paper 4 Writing and Paper 1 Speaking** are the opposite: the instructions are in English, and everything you write or say is in **French**.

**Answering comprehension questions well**:

- Give **exactly what is asked** — if the question asks for one reason, one reason is enough; a list risks contradicting itself.
- Include the **detail**: a time, a number, a reason, a negative. *He does not play football* is a different answer from *he plays football*.
- Watch the **negatives**: *ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … plus* reverse a sentence, and a listener hunting for familiar nouns misses them.
- Watch the **tense**: *j'ai joué* (did), *je joue* (does), *je vais jouer* (will) are three different answers.

**Don't translate the whole text.** Comprehension marks come from finding the answer, not from rendering every sentence. Save full translation for the question that actually asks for it.

steps.title: Translation into English
steps.body: The Reading paper ends with a translation into English: one passage at Higher, five sentences at Foundation. The method is to account for every word first, then make the English natural.

visuals.problem: Translate: « Quand j'étais petite, je n'aimais pas le collège. Maintenant j'y vais avec plaisir, parce que j'ai de meilleures notes. J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans. »

steps.text: *Quand j'étais petite* → **When I was little** — imperfect, and *petite* shows a female speaker.
*je n'aimais pas le collège* → **I did not like school** — the negative must survive the translation.
*Maintenant j'y vais avec plaisir* → **Now I go there happily** — *y* is *there*, and must be translated.
steps.note: a small word still carries a mark

steps.text: *parce que j'ai de meilleures notes* → **because I get better marks** — *meilleures* is *better*, not *more good*.
*J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans* → **I have been learning French for five years** — present + *depuis* becomes an English perfect.
steps.note: the tense changes shape in English

check.prompt: Translate into English: **je n'aimais pas le collège**.
check.solution: **I did not like school.** *Aimais* is the imperfect, so the English is past: *I do not like school* loses the tense. *Ne … pas* must survive, so *I liked school* says the opposite. *Collège* is secondary school, not college: *I did not like college* falls for a false friend.
options: I do not like school
I did not like school
I liked school
I did not like college

steps.title: Le speaking et la dictée
steps.body:
**Paper 1 has three tasks, always in this order.**

**1. Read aloud** — a short French text read out, then a short interaction. Worth **12 of 50** marks at both tiers: 8 for reading aloud, 4 for answering two unprepared questions. Read French *as French*: leave the silent endings silent (*ils jouent* sounds like *il joue*), make the liaisons (*les_enfants*), keep the nasal vowels (*on, en, un*), and use the text's own punctuation for phrasing.

**2. Role play** — you play a part in a set situation and respond in French to each prompt. **Every prompt must be covered**; one skipped prompt is marks gone. At least one prompt always says *ask a question* (one at Foundation, two at Higher), so have *À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Est-ce que vous avez… ?* ready.

**3. Picture task** — choose one of two photos and describe the **people**, the **location** and the **activity**; answer two unprepared questions (at Higher the second is in a past tense); then a conversation on the same theme. A shape that works is **describe, then give an opinion, then bring in a second tense**: *Sur la photo, il y a… · À mon avis, c'est… parce que… · Moi, l'année dernière, j'ai…*

**Preparation**: 15 minutes — 14 in the invigilation room, then **1 minute in the exam room to practise the read aloud out loud**.

**The dictation** (Listening Section B): a short French passage, played **3 times** with pauses between sentences, written down in French. Spelling, accents and **silent endings** all count — the *-ent* you never hear, the agreement you cannot hear, the final consonant that stays silent but must be written.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the four papers and say what each is worth.
2. Which parts of the exam are answered in English?
3. How many times is the dictation played?

**Part B.**

4. Translate into English: *je ne vais jamais au cinéma*.
5. Write three questions you could use for the "ask a question" prompt in a role play.
6. Write the three-part shape of a good picture-task answer.

**Part C.**

7. Translate into English, accounting for every word: *quand j'étais petit, je n'avais pas de portable, mais maintenant j'en ai un*.
8. Write down what you would do with each of the three dictation hearings.
9. Plan a revision week: which paper you would work on each day, and how.

For question 7, check the tense and the negative both survive into your English.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Check the language of the question, every time.** English question, English answer. It costs nothing and it is the single biggest avoidable loss in the exam.

**Listen for the words that change the meaning.** *Ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … plus*, and the tense markers *hier, demain, avant*. A candidate hunting for familiar nouns hears *foot* and *samedi* and writes the opposite of what was said.

**Account for every word in the translation.** Small words — *y, en, déjà, encore, ne … que* — each carry meaning. Translate them, then reread the English on its own and make it sound like English.

**Change the tense shape where English needs it.** *J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans* is *I **have been** learning*, not *I learn*. *Je jouais* is *I used to play* or *I was playing*. This is where the translation marks are won.

**Use the read aloud preparation minute.** Say the text out loud once, and pick out the words with silent endings, liaisons and nasal vowels before they count. 12 of 50 speaking marks sit in that one task, 8 of them for pronunciation.

**Cover every role-play prompt.** A prompt you skip is a mark you cannot get back, and the "ask a question" prompt is the one candidates most often forget.

**Build the picture task in three moves.** Describe the people, the location and the activity, then an opinion with a reason, then a second tense. At Higher the teacher's second question is in a past tense, so have one ready.

**Use all three dictation hearings differently.** Listening three times the same way wastes two of them.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Four papers**, 50 marks and **25%** each: Speaking, Listening, Reading, Writing — 200 marks in all.
- **Speaking** (Higher 10–12 min, Foundation 7–9, after **15 minutes** preparation, the last **1** in the exam room): read aloud (**12** marks), role play (**10**), picture task (**28**).
- **Listening** (Higher 60 min, Foundation 45): Section A in English, Section B a **dictation** in French, played **3** times.
- **Reading** (Higher 60 min, Foundation 45): English questions and answers, plus a **translation into English**.
- **Writing** (Higher 80 min, Foundation 75): English instructions, French answers; **80–90** words for the informal task, **130–150** for the Higher formal task, **40–50** for the Foundation formal task.
- **English question → English answer.** The specification requires all responses in English there.
- Give the **detail**: times, numbers, reasons, negatives.
- Watch *ne … pas / jamais / plus* and the tense markers.
- In translation, **account for every word**, then make the English natural.
- *Depuis* + present → *have been doing*; imperfect → *used to / was doing*.
- Role play: **cover every prompt**, including *ask a question*.
- Picture task: **describe · opinion with a reason · a second tense**.
- Dictation: whole sentence, then gaps, then check accents and silent endings.

80–90 words; 130–150 for the Higher formal task

questions.prompt: A listening question asks why Marc did not go out. The recording says "*je ne suis pas sorti parce que j'étais malade*". What is the answer?
options: He went out with a friend
He did not want to go out
He was tired after school
He was ill
questions.solution: *Parce que j'étais malade* — **he was ill**. The negative *ne … pas* confirms he did not go out; the reason is what the question asks for.

questions.prompt: Translate into English, accounting for every word: **quand j'étais petit, je n'avais pas de portable, mais maintenant j'en ai un**.
questions.solution: **When I was little, I didn't have a mobile, but now I have one.** The imperfect (*étais*, *avais*), the negative and *en* (*one*) all have to appear. *I had a mobile* loses the negative; *I have some* misreads *j'en ai un*, which is *I have one*; *When I am little, I don't have* turns the imperfect into a present.

French answers are marked on a different paper instead
The examiner is not allowed to read French on that paper
It would count as translation, which is a separate question
questions.solution: Reading assesses **understanding**, demonstrated in English: The specification says all questions are set in English and students produce all responses in English. Copying French words from the text does not show the examiner you understood them.

questions.prompt: Translate into English: **je jouais au foot tous les samedis, mais je me suis blessé, donc je ne joue plus**.
questions.solution: **I used to play football every Saturday, but I hurt myself, so I don't play any more.** Three things must survive: the imperfect habit (*I play football* loses it), the reflexive *je me suis blessé* (*I hurt him* misreads the pronoun) and *ne … plus* as *no longer* (*so I still play* reverses it).

questions.prompt: Which answer to a picture task describes the picture, gives an opinion with a reason and uses a second tense?
options: Sur la photo, il y a une famille à table. À mon avis, c'est important parce qu'on discute. Hier, on a mangé au restaurant.
À mon avis, c'est important de manger ensemble parce qu'on discute beaucoup et on se raconte notre journée.
Sur la photo, il y a une famille à table, une cuisine, une fenêtre, des assiettes, un chien et des verres.
Hier, on a mangé au restaurant, et demain on va manger chez ma tante avec toute la famille et mes cousins.
questions.solution: **Describe, then an opinion with a reason, then a second tense.** Only the answer that starts *Sur la photo, il y a une famille à table* does all three. The one that is all *à mon avis* never describes the photo, the list of objects is description only, and the one about *hier* and *demain* never describes the photo either.

examTechnique.body:
Four papers, **50 marks and 25% each**, so none can be neglected. **Check the language of the question**: English questions take English answers, and in Writing and Speaking the instructions are in English but everything you produce is in French.

In comprehension give the **detail** asked for and listen for the negatives and tense markers. In translation **account for every word**, then make the English natural. In speaking, cover **every** role-play prompt, build the picture task as *describe · opinion with a reason · a second tense*, and spend the exam-room minute saying the read aloud out loud.
examinerErrors: Answering in French where the question is in English.
Missing a negative and giving the opposite answer.
Leaving a word or phrase out of the translation.
Translating depuis + present as a simple present.
Skipping a role-play prompt, usually the question.
Describing a photo with no opinion or second tense.
Using all three dictation hearings in the same way.
Revising only the papers you enjoy.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 candidate checks the language of every question before writing, answers comprehension with exactly the detail asked for, and hears *ne … pas*, *jamais* and *plus* as the words that decide the answer. In translation every word is accounted for and the tenses are reshaped into natural English — *depuis* + present as *have been doing*, the imperfect as *used to*. In speaking, every role-play prompt is covered including the question, the picture task runs description, opinion with a reason, then a second tense, and the preparation minute is spent saying the read aloud out loud.
